items.title: Ice Logo
items.excerpt: Any SVG logo cut from ice: it crumbles into splinters, chips and powder under the cursor, then pieces itself back together.
items.summary: Any SVG logo cut from ice: it crumbles under the cursor, then pieces itself back together.
items.body:
Ice Logo

 Any SVG logo cut from ice: it crumbles into splinters, chips and powder under the cursor, then pieces itself back together.

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/ice-logo/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/ice-logo/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/ice-logo/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/ice-logo/params.json

Ice Logo turns any SVG logo into a block of ice. Move the cursor over it and the ice cracks into splinters, chips and powder, then the pieces fly back and the logo heals itself. We first built it for a client's brand page, then made the logo an input so the same effect works for any mark.

How it works

The logo stays one solid mesh until it breaks. The SVG is read with Three.js's SVGLoader, centred, and scaled so its larger side is always the same length. That way the tuned values (depth, bevel, reach) look the same for a wide wordmark and a square icon. The shapes are then extruded into one smooth, bevelled mesh.

The cracks are planned before anything breaks. Points are scattered over the logo and turned into Voronoi cells with d3-delaunay, then stretched so they read as splinters rather than tiles. Each cell is clipped to the logo outline with polygon-clipping. Which cells are broken is stored in a small texture, and the shader on the intact mesh cuts a hole wherever a cell is marked broken.

Each broken cell has a hidden twin. For every cell there's a jagged chunk, hidden until its cell breaks. Then it flies out with a push, a spin and gravity, and a spring pulls it back to its place. When it lands, the hole closes and the chunk hides again. Powder and small chips are drawn from fixed pools, so a burst of breaking never allocates new objects mid-animation.

The ice is a physical material. It uses Three.js's transmission (glass) material with frost textures drawn on a canvas at startup. The frost changes as the logo turns toward or away from the light, so the ice moves between cloudy and see-through while the cursor moves.

When to use it

If a brand page has one hero moment and a logo that people will play with, it works well: it rewards the cursor without asking for a click.

If the page is long, or the logo sits next to text people need to read, keep it smaller or use something lighter. The effect runs WebGL with a glass material, so it costs more than a CSS animation, and on low-end phones it is worth lowering cells and dust.

Every value in the tuning app is also a data- attribute on the embed, so what you set in the app is what you ship.

items.title: Ripple Reveal
items.excerpt: Slideshow transition using CSS mask + radial-gradient to expand slides outward from a configurable origin point with a soft liquid ripple edge
items.summary: Each new slide spreads out from one point with a soft, liquid edge.
items.body:
Ripple Reveal

 Slideshow transition using CSS mask + radial-gradient to expand slides outward from a configurable origin point with a soft liquid ripple edge

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal/params.json

CSS mask + radial-gradient expands the incoming slide outward from a configurable origin point. A single @property --p drives the radius; a feather zone between the two gradient stops creates a soft, liquid ripple edge.

Ripple reveal

Circle expands from a configurable origin, like a drop hitting still water. The slideshow auto-advances every 5 seconds with a 1.2s reveal animation.

How it works

The key is @property --p — a registered CSS custom property that can be animated with @keyframes. Without @property, animating --p inside radial-gradient() doesn't work because the browser can't interpolate unregistered custom properties.

 

The active slide computes a radius from --p, then derives two edge stops for a feather zone:

 

The --feather gap between --edge-in and --edge-out softens the expanding ring. Larger values → blurrier edge; 0 → hard circle wipe.

The origin and timing are params (data- attributes on the embed, options in code). The class writes them to custom properties on the slideshow container:

 

The time between slides (delay, in ms) stays in JS.

150% for the max radius guarantees the circle covers all four corners regardless of origin position. If you set originX: 0, the farthest corner is the top-right; 150% of the diagonal still clears it.

Slide z-index management

CSS animation doesn't handle stacking — JS does. Each transition bumps a monotonically increasing zCounter so the incoming slide always paints above everything:

 

The remove + add in sequence forces the browser to restart the @keyframes animation even if the slide was previously .active. After animDuration + 200ms (the duration param), the previous slide drops its .active class and falls to z-index: 0.

Ken Burns effect

Active slides get a slow scale(1.1) via a long transition:

 

The 10s duration means the zoom is barely perceptible within a 5s slide hold, but visible as slow drift — the Ken Burns effect without JS.

Accessibility

 

When prefers-reduced-motion is set, skip mounting the slideshow entirely so slides don't auto-advance and no animation runs.

Top-left origin

Set originX: 0 and originY: 0 (data-origin-x="0" data-origin-y="0" on the embed) — ripple expands from the top-left corner.

params.label: Time between slides
params.help: Milliseconds a slide stays before the next one ripples in.

params.label: Reveal duration
params.help: Milliseconds one reveal takes.

params.label: Feather
params.help: Width of the soft edge. 0 is a hard circle.

params.label: Origin X
params.help: Where the ripple starts across the width. 0 is the left edge.

params.label: Origin Y
params.help: Where the ripple starts down the height. 0 is the top edge.

params.label: Ease
params.help: Speed curve of the expansion.

params.label: Drift zoom
params.help: Scale the image slowly grows to while shown. 1 turns it off.

params.label: Background
params.help: Colour behind the slides.

items.title: Ripple Reveal WebGL
items.excerpt: Slideshow transition using WebGL with radial mask crossfade and Gaussian sine ring distortion for true pixel-level wave refraction at the reveal edge
items.summary: Slides change with a water ripple that bends the image at its edge.
items.body:
Ripple Reveal WebGL

 Slideshow transition using WebGL with radial mask crossfade and Gaussian sine ring distortion for true pixel-level wave refraction at the reveal edge

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal-webgl/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal-webgl/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal-webgl/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/ripple-reveal-webgl/params.json

WebGL canvas replaces CSS mask entirely. A fragment shader crossfades two slide textures behind a radial mask while Gaussian-enveloped sine rings physically distort pixels at the wave front — true refractive warping, not a visual overlay.

Ripple reveal WebGL

Circle expands from a configurable origin, distorting image pixels at the wave edge like light refracting through moving water.

Top-left origin

Set originX: 0, originY: 0 (or data-origin-x="0" data-origin-y="0") — the same shader handles any origin.

How it works

A fullscreen <canvas element replaces all slide markup. One GLSL fragment shader does everything in a single pass:

1. Compute aspect-correct distance from each pixel to the wave origin
2. Apply Gaussian-enveloped sine ring distortion near the wave front
3. Sample both slide textures at the displaced UV coordinates
4. Mix prev/curr via a smoothstep radial mask

Ring distortion

 

x = dist - radius is negative ahead of the wave, zero at the front, positive behind. The Gaussian bell (band) ensures only pixels close to the wave front get displaced — the effect stays confined to the ring, not the whole image.

The trailing wake (x < 0) uses a different envelope: exponential decay scaled by decay. At decay: 0 the exponential collapses to zero instantly, giving a clean leading edge only. At decay: 3 (default) the distortion fades out slowly behind the wave like a comet tail.

Radial mask crossfade

 

smoothstep produces the soft feather zone. maxDist 0.75 covers the farthest corner from any origin position.

Params → WebGL uniforms

 

Every value lives in params.ts and reaches the shader as a uniform. The values are read every frame, so setParams({ ringSpeed: 2 }) takes effect without a restart.

Texture management

All slide images preload into WebGL textures before the first frame:

 

gl.UNPACKFLIPYWEBGL flips Y on upload so UV (0,0) maps to the image top-left (matching CSS convention).

Ken Burns zoom

UV scaling in the shader — no CSS transform needed:

 

uKenBurnsCurr goes 0→0.1 during the transition; uKenBurnsPrev stays fixed at 0.1 (outgoing slide is already fully zoomed). Both run from their own independent clocks so the outgoing slide doesn't stutter when a new transition begins.

Accessibility

 

Skip mount() entirely — don't just reduce duration. The Ken Burns zoom alone can trigger vestibular symptoms at full speed.

params.label: Origin Y

items.title: Venetian Blind
items.excerpt: Two CSS mask transitions that split a slide into vertical strips — one collapses the outgoing image, the other reveals the incoming one. No JS animation library.
items.summary: Slides change in vertical strips, like a blind turning open.
items.body:
Venetian Blind

 Two CSS mask transitions that split a slide into vertical strips — one collapses the outgoing image, the other reveals the incoming one. No JS animation library.

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/venetian-blind/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/venetian-blind/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/venetian-blind/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/venetian-blind/params.json

Two variations of a venetian-blind transition for full-bleed image slideshows — both built entirely with CSS mask and @keyframes, no animation library. The effect splits a slide into 5 vertical strips that collapse or expand with a staggered timing, creating a mechanical reveal that works well for editorial and portfolio contexts.

Disappear: outgoing slide collapses

Each strip on the outgoing slide shrinks toward its vertical center, exposing the next image beneath.

Five @property-registered custom properties (--p1…--p5) animate from 0 to 1 via @keyframes. Each drives a column of the mask, shrinking the visible region toward center:

 

The +1px on column width closes rasterization gaps at non-integer device pixel ratios. .active goes on the outgoing slide (direction: "collapse"); after animationend it's removed and the slide drops to z-index: 0.

Reveal: incoming slide expands

Same strips, reversed direction — the incoming slide expands outward from center rather than collapsing inward.

Two things differ from the disappear variant:

1. .active targets the incoming slide, not the outgoing. The outgoing stays at z-index: 1 beneath, fully visible until covered.
2. Strip formula is inverted: starts at center, expands to edges.

 

With direction: "reveal" non-active slides have no mask applied — they're fully visible by default. Only the incoming .active slide carries the mask during its animation.

In the packaged effect both variants are one class, switched by the direction param. A single @property --vm-vb-p runs 0 to 1 over duration, and the mask built for each slide derives every strip's own progress from it (stagger percent later per strip, eased in as t squared), so the strip count is a param too. The direction is purely determined by the --t/--b formula.

Why @property

Custom properties are strings by default — they can't be interpolated by @keyframes. Registering them as <number via @property makes them numeric and animatable:

 

Without this, the mask would snap from start to end on the first frame instead of animating.

Why no JS animation library

The script only manages state: track current index, raise the animated slide's z-index, toggle .active. All interpolation happens in CSS. Zero dependencies.

Accessibility

 

When prefers-reduced-motion is set, skip mount and keep the first image as a static <img. Slides stay static.

params.label: Direction
params.help: Whether the outgoing strips shrink to their centre or the incoming strips grow from it.

params.label: Strips
params.help: Number of vertical strips.

params.label: Stagger
params.help: How far each strip lags the one before it, as a percentage of the transition. 0 moves them together.

params.label: Transition duration
params.help: Milliseconds one transition takes.

params.label: Time between slides
params.help: Milliseconds a slide stays before the next transition.

items.title: CSS Tab Shape
items.excerpt: Create tab shapes using CSS mask and clip-path: shape() techniques
items.summary: Folder-style tabs with curved corners, cut in plain CSS.
items.body:
CSS Tab Shape

 Create tab shapes using CSS mask and clip-path: shape() techniques

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/css-tab-shape/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/css-tab-shape/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/css-tab-shape/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/css-tab-shape/params.json

Create tab shapes using CSS mask and clip-path: shape() techniques.

Tab UI with CSS mask

1. Apply normal paddings
2. Create a border around the tab, as we will mask out everything from this border outward.
 
3. Use mask with 3 layers to cut out the red border
 
4. Finish with hover status

Clip path shape()
This approach using clip-path: shape(), a modern function of clip path. This solve the box model issue of using mask.

 
Tabs with folder shape

params.help: Folder: shape() with a slanted right edge. Clip-path: shape() with flared feet. Mask: a border cut away with mask layers.

items.title: Horizontal Sticky Stack
items.excerpt: A vanilla CSS horizontal scroll section where cards stick and stack as you scroll through.
items.summary: Cards slide in sideways and stack on top of each other as you scroll.
items.body:
Horizontal Sticky Stack

 A vanilla CSS horizontal scroll section where cards stick and stack as you scroll through.

Live: https://vanilla-motion.com/horizontal-sticky-stack/ · Tuning app: https://vanilla-motion.com/horizontal-sticky-stack/app/ · Code reference: https://vanilla-motion.com/horizontal-sticky-stack/skill.md · Params: https://vanilla-motion.com/horizontal-sticky-stack/params.json

A scroll-driven layout where cards pin in place and stack horizontally as the user scrolls down. This pattern creates a sense of depth and sequence, commonly used for feature showcases and product walkthroughs.

What makes this tutorial special: the motion is pure CSS using animation- — no JavaScript runs while you scroll. (The effect's small script only builds the cards and writes your settings as CSS variables.) Note that scroll-driven animations are not supported on Firefox at the time of this writing.

Step 1: The first stack

My approach for complex layouts always starts with the static layout and a proper box model first.

Step 2: Static, responsive layout

Then proceed with the complete layout for both desktop and mobile. No need to put 100% effort into this step — it's just a prep so we have in mind how the mobile layout will look.

 At this step, since we are aware that there's animation to apply, be a bit more generous with HTML elements — allow more wrappers, each handling a specific purpose. One wrapper for sticky, one for sizing with width and height, one for transform. This helps avoid CSS conflicts in the animation steps.

Step 3: Sticky

Here comes the fun part. Implement the animation once the static layout is ready.

params.label: Layout
